title: Neurodiversity at Work: Practical Kindness Beats Perfect Policy
subtitle: Clear communication, flexibility, and thoughtful team habits help people do their best work.

intro.title: Different Brains, Shared Workplace
paragraphs: Roughly 15 to 20% of people are neurodivergent. Neurodiversity is a natural variation in how brains process information, communicate, and solve problems.
Most workplace norms were built around neurotypical defaults. That can unintentionally create friction for people who process language, pace, or social interaction differently.
Support is not about lowering expectations. It is about removing avoidable barriers so people can contribute their strengths in meaningful, high-impact ways.

blocks.title: Four Practical Changes Leaders Can Make Right Away

items.title: 1) Lead with clear communication
items.body: Share agendas ahead of time, define decisions clearly, and write down action items. This reduces guesswork and helps everyone prepare in a way that fits their processing style.

items.title: 2) Make expectations explicit
items.body: Do not rely on unwritten rules. Clarify what done means, response-time expectations, and escalation paths so no one has to decode hidden norms.

items.title: 3) Offer flexibility in how work gets done
items.body: Some people think best out loud, others need quiet processing time and written follow-ups. Design team workflows that allow multiple communication paths.

callout.text: When people can process information in their best format, output quality usually improves for the whole team.

items.title: 4) Normalize strength-based support
items.body: A person may need more time in one area and still be exceptional in others, such as pattern recognition, systems thinking, creativity, empathy, or connecting ideas others miss.

items.title: What I know
items.body: As someone who is dyslexic and dysgraphic, I know I will not be the fastest reader in the room, and rapid-fire discussions can be hard.

items.title: What I have learned
items.body: That same processing style can also support deeper pattern recognition, creative problem solving, and stronger empathy in technical and human systems.

items.title: What teams can do
items.body: Patience, written follow-ups, clear structure, and psychological safety help people share what works for them and contribute at a higher level.

items.title: Not this
items.body: How do we make this person fit our existing process?

items.title: Try this
items.body: Which parts of our process create avoidable friction, and how can we redesign them?

items.title: Result
items.body: More clarity, less hidden effort, and better outcomes for everyone.

blocks.title: Final Thought
paragraphs: Inclusion is not a single policy. It is hundreds of small decisions made every week.
When leaders combine clarity, flexibility, and care, teams become both more humane and more effective.

footer.heading: Design For Humans, Not Just Throughput
footer.text: Teams that feel safe to think differently usually build better things.
